statement: The rectangle contained by rational straight lines commensurable in square only is irrational, and the side of the square equal to it is irrational. Let the latter be called medial.
heath_proof: For let the rectangle AC be contained by the rational straight lines AB, BC commensurable in square only; I say that AC is irrational, and the side of the square equal to it is irrational; and let the latter be called medial. For on AB let the square AD be described; therefore AD is rational. [X. Def. 4] And, since AB is incommensurable in length with BC, for by hypothesis they are commensurable in square only, while AB is equal to BD, therefore DB is also incommensurable in length with BC. And, as DB is to BC, so is AD to AC; [VI. 1] therefore DA is incommensurable with AC. [X. 11] But DA is rational; therefore AC is irrational, so that the side of the square equal to AC is also irrational. [X. Def. 4] And let the latter be called medial.

**Statement:** The rectangle contained by rational straight lines commensurable in square only is irrational, and the side of the square equal to it is irrational. Let the latter be called medial.

**Step 1.** Let AB, BC be rational straight lines commensurable in square only (D10.1.3, D10.1.2), and let AC be the rectangle contained by AB, BC (D2.1), so that the angle ABC is right. I say that the rectangle AC is irrational, and that the side of the square equal to AC is irrational.

**Step 2.** On AB describe the square AD (1.46), placing it on the side of AB remote from C; let its vertices be A, B, D, E. Since AD is a square, BD is equal to AB and the angle ABD is right (D1.22).

**Step 3.** With the straight line AB, at the point B on it, the two straight lines BD, BC lie on opposite sides of AB and make the adjacent angles ABD, ABC, each of which is right; hence these adjacent angles are together equal to two right angles. Therefore DB is in a straight line with BC (1.14), and D, B, C lie on one straight line DC.

**Step 4.** The square AD is rational. For AB is rational, that is, it is commensurable with the assigned rational straight line, whether in length and in square or in square only (D10.1.3); in either case AB is commensurable in square with the assigned straight line, so that the square on AB and the square on the assigned straight line are measured by the same area (D10.1.2), i.e. they are commensurable. But the square on the assigned straight line is rational, and areas commensurable with it are rational (D10.1.4). Therefore the square AD, being the square on AB, is rational.

**Step 5.** Since AB, BC are commensurable in square only, they are not commensurable in length, so that AB and BC have no common measure (D10.1.1). And BD is equal to AB (Step 2); hence any magnitude measuring both DB and BC would measure both AB and BC. Therefore DB is incommensurable in length with BC (D10.1.1).

**Step 6.** The square AD and the rectangle AC are parallelograms whose bases DB, BC lie on the one straight line DC (Step 3), and each has the same height, namely the perpendicular AB drawn from the common vertex A to the base (D6.4), since the angles ABD, ABC are right. Therefore, as DB is to BC, so is the square AD to the rectangle AC (6.1).

**Step 7.** Thus the four magnitudes DB, BC, AD, AC are proportional, and the first, DB, is incommensurable with the second, BC (Step 5). Therefore the third, the square AD, is incommensurable with the fourth, the rectangle AC (10.11).

**Step 8.** Now the square AD is rational (Step 4); that is, AD and the square on the assigned rational straight line are two commensurable magnitudes, and one of them, AD, is incommensurable with the magnitude AC (Step 7). Therefore the remaining one, the square on the assigned straight line, is also incommensurable with AC (10.13). But areas incommensurable with the square on the assigned straight line are irrational (D10.1.4). Therefore the rectangle AC is irrational.

**Step 9.** Let a square be constructed equal to the rectangle AC (2.14), and let G be its side. The rectangle AC is not itself a square but another rectilineal figure, and it is irrational; therefore the straight line G, on which is described a square equal to AC, is irrational (D10.1.4).

**Step 10.** Therefore the rectangle contained by rational straight lines commensurable in square only is irrational, and the side of the square equal to it is irrational. Let the latter be called medial. Q.E.D.
